prompts.history.timeline.short: Make a timeline for “[topic]”: 8–10 key dates.
prompts.history.timeline.detailed: Make a timeline table for “[topic]” covering [period]. Columns: date, event, why it matters (one sentence), which later event it connects to. If an exact date is disputed or approximate, say so. Don't add events you're unsure about.
prompts.history.timeline.refine: Cut it down to the 5 events you can't understand the topic without, and explain the choice.
prompts.history.timeline.check: Shuffle the events from the timeline and I'll put them in order. Then check.
prompts.history.causes.short: List the causes and consequences of: [event]
prompts.history.causes.detailed: Analyse the event “[event]”. Split the causes into long-term causes and the immediate trigger, and the consequences into short-term and long-term. One sentence of explanation for each item. Separately note which items historians disagree on.
prompts.history.causes.refine: Which cause would you say is the main one? Give arguments for and against.
prompts.history.causes.check: Here's my answer on the causes: [answer]. What did I miss, and where am I confusing a cause with the trigger?
prompts.history.periods.detailed: Compare [period 1] and [period 2] in the history of [country or region]. Table by criteria: government, economy, society, culture, relations with neighbours. 1–2 sentences and an example in each cell. Below the table: what changed most and what stayed the same.
prompts.history.periods.refine: Add the criterion [criterion] and explain why it matters for the comparison.
prompts.history.periods.check: Ask 5 “which period does this belong to?” questions from this table. Check my answers.
prompts.history.source.short: Help me analyse a historical source: [source text]
prompts.history.source.detailed: Help me analyse a source. What I know about it: [author, date, type]. Text: [source text]. Go through these questions: who made it and why, for whom, what it says directly, what can be read between the lines, what's missing, how far it can be trusted and why. Rely only on the text and what I've told you.
prompts.history.source.refine: What other sources should I compare this one with to check it? Name types, not specific documents.
prompts.history.source.check: Here's my analysis: [analysis]. Where am I just retelling and where am I actually analysing?
prompts.history.answer.short: Make an answer outline for the question: [question]
prompts.history.answer.detailed: Make an outline for an extended answer to “[question]” for [lesson, exam or essay]. 4–6 points: introduction with a thesis, main parts noting which fact or example belongs there, conclusion. Don't write the full answer: I want to write it myself.
prompts.history.answer.refine: Which 3 dates or names must I mention in this answer?
prompts.history.answer.check: Here's my answer: [answer]. Rate it on thesis, facts, logic, conclusion. What should I improve first?
prompts.history.views.short: What viewpoints exist on [event or issue]?
prompts.history.views.detailed: Describe different viewpoints on “[event or issue]”. Table: position, its main argument, the facts it relies on, the objections to it. Present each position fairly and in its strongest form, without your own verdict. If you're not sure who held it, don't name anyone.
prompts.history.views.refine: Why do these viewpoints differ so much? Is it the sources, the time or the authors' outlook?
prompts.history.views.check: I lean towards [position]. What are the strongest arguments against it that I should address?
prompts.history.concept.short: Explain the concept “[concept]” in simple words with an example.
prompts.history.concept.detailed: Explain the concept “[concept]” for [grade or course]. Structure: definition, its features as a list, an example from history or today, how it differs from the similar concept [similar concept], how to use it in a class answer.
prompts.history.concept.refine: Give two examples: one that fits the concept and one that looks similar but doesn't. Explain the difference.
prompts.history.concept.check: Check my definition: [definition]. Which feature is missing?
prompts.history.verify.short: Check the dates and names in my text: [text]
prompts.history.verify.detailed: List all dates, names, titles and numbers from my text. Table: what's stated, whether it seems right, how confident you are (high, medium, low), where to check it. If unsure, don't correct it, mark it “check”. Text: [text]
prompts.history.verify.refine: For the low-confidence items, write search queries so I can check them myself.
prompts.history.verify.check: I checked in my textbook: [check results]. Update the table and mark where you were wrong.
prompts.history.overview.short: Give a short overview of “[topic]” in 7 points.
prompts.history.overview.detailed: Make an overview of “[topic]” for review before [lesson or exam]. Structure: context in 2–3 sentences, key events, key people and their role, main concepts, outcomes and significance. No more than one page.
prompts.history.overview.refine: Turn the overview into 10 self-check questions, from facts to understanding.
prompts.history.overview.check: I'll retell the topic from memory: [retelling]. What important points did I miss?
prompts.history.interpretation.short: What in this text is fact and what is interpretation? [text]
prompts.history.interpretation.detailed: Analyse a text about the past: [text]. Table: phrase, type (fact, interpretation, judgement), which words show it, how it could be checked. Explain which words usually signal interpretation, such as “proves”, “the main cause”, “unfortunately”.
prompts.history.interpretation.refine: Rewrite interpretation [number] neutrally, keeping only checkable facts.
prompts.history.interpretation.check: Here's how I marked it: [my marks]. Where do you disagree and why?

verify.history.timeline: Check every date against your textbook or an encyclopedia: AI may shift a year or mix up events.
verify.history.causes: Historical events usually have many causes, and historians weigh them differently. Compare with your textbook.
verify.history.periods: A comparison is a generalisation. Find an example in your textbook for each point, otherwise the conclusion may be a stretch.
verify.history.source: The AI doesn't know whether your source is genuine or where it came from. Take its origin and date from your textbook or document collection.
verify.history.answer: The outline is a support, not a finished answer. Take the facts for each point from your textbook and notes.
verify.history.views: AI may attribute a position to someone who never held it. Find the viewpoints in your textbook or in the named historians' work.
verify.history.concept: Definitions of social concepts vary between textbooks and laws. For your answer, use your textbook's wording.
verify.history.verify: The AI's answer here only tells you what to check. Verify finally against a textbook, encyclopedia or archival publication.
verify.history.overview: The AI's overview may leave out things that matter for your syllabus. Compare it with the section headings in your textbook.
verify.history.interpretation: The line between fact and interpretation isn't always obvious. Discuss borderline cases with your teacher.
